findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive and exact-match
findings.body: `should_block?` uses `where(email: email)` with the raw input. A user can get past a block by changing letter case (e.g. `Bad@spammers.org`), because the check runs before the email is normalized. Normalize both the stored and the checked email (downcase and strip) before comparing.

findings.title: Non-atomic match_count increment loses updates
findings.body: `should_block?` reads the record, adds 1 in Ruby, then saves. Concurrent signups can overwrite each other's increments. It also runs a full save with validations, including a uniqueness query, on every validation. Use `update_all` or `increment_counter` instead.

findings.title: Validation has side effects that inflate statistics
findings.body: `should_block?` writes match statistics every time the validator runs. The users controller calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, so validation runs twice per signup and each blocked match is counted twice. Every `valid?` call anywhere also mutates the database.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array shared across controller instances
findings.body: `Em.A([])` is defined on the prototype in `extend`, so every instance of the controller shares the same array. Initialize it in `init` instead.

findings.title: Any email error permanently rejects the address client-side
findings.body: Any email error is treated as a permanent rejection, including transient ones such as 'already taken'. The address is then marked invalid with no way to retry it without reloading the page.
